title: The 3 AM Phone Call
tagline: Your first server will always fail
story: Launch day. One VPS, one MySQL install, one dream. The site is live and the first merchant signs up.
At 3:07 AM your phone rings. The server is dead and a customer is already tweeting about it.
You have no monitoring, no alerts, no idea how long it has been down.

scenes.prompt: The phone is buzzing on the nightstand. What do you reach for first?

choices.label: Set up monitoring before touching anything
choices.detail: Uptime checks, alerting to your phone, a status page. Boring. Non-negotiable.
choices.result: By sunrise you know exactly what died, when, and why: the disk filled up. You fix it in nine minutes instead of nine hours.
choices.lesson: Your first server will always fail. It's not a matter of if, but when. The goal is to know before your customers do.

choices.label: SSH in, restart everything, buy a bigger server
choices.detail: Brute force. It works today.
choices.result: The site comes back up at 3:40 AM. You promise yourself you'll add monitoring 'next week'. You won't.
choices.lesson: Your first server will always fail. Restarting without understanding is how 3 AM calls become weekly rituals.

choices.label: Silence the phone. Deal with it in the morning.
choices.detail: It's probably fine. Right?
choices.result: It was down for six hours. Your first ten merchants experienced their launch week as an outage. Some never came back.
choices.lesson: Downtime compounds: every silent minute burns trust you haven't earned yet.

title: The WhatsApp PDF Problem
tagline: The origin story of the MVP
story: Sellers like Priya run shops with no website. They photograph products, make PDF catalogs, and WhatsApp them to customers. Orders happen in chat, chaos happens in accounting.
You see the problem clearly. Now everyone wants to know when the 'real product' ships.
Your co-founder wants a perfect platform. Your bank account disagrees.

choices.label: Ship the ugly MVP now
choices.detail: One screen: catalog as a shareable page, orders land in a simple admin. Ugly but alive.
choices.result: Priya shares her catalog link in three WhatsApp groups. By Friday, forty sellers signed up out of nowhere. The experiment worked — people want this.
choices.lesson: The MVP is an experiment to test your core hypothesis, not a small version of the final product.

choices.label: Build the real platform properly first
choices.detail: Multi-tenant, beautiful dashboards, mobile apps. Six months, minimum.
choices.result: Six months later you launch something polished... for a market that has already moved. Competitors shipped ugly and learned fast.
choices.lesson: Perfect is the enemy of tested. An unshipped product teaches you nothing about the market.

choices.label: Outsource to the cheapest agency you can find
choices.detail: They promise 'full e-commerce solution' in one month.
choices.result: It launches. Sort of. Every page load rolls dice, and the codebase arrives as a zip file with zero documentation. You inherit the mess.
choices.lesson: Technical debt taken on day one charges interest during every future crisis.

title: The Great Divorce
tagline: Separating the app and the database
story: Growth is real now. But every traffic spike makes the whole site slow — because your app and your database live on the same machine, fighting for the same CPU.
Postgres is eating 95% of the box while the app server starves next to it.

scenes.prompt: How do you split them up?

choices.label: Move the database to its own server
choices.detail: Two machines, each doing what it's best at. Tuned Postgres, dedicated resources.
choices.result: Latency drops by half overnight. The app breathes, the database breathes, and for the first time they can scale independently.
choices.lesson: Separating your application and database servers is the first crucial step in scaling.

choices.label: Buy a bigger single box. Again.
choices.detail: Vertical scaling forever. What could go wrong?
choices.result: Faster... until the next spike. And now the price of your 'temporary' fix is permanent, with a single point of failure attached.
choices.lesson: Vertical scaling buys time, not architecture. There is always a ceiling — and you are racing toward it.

choices.label: Just run more app processes on the same box
choices.detail: Free capacity, right? Squeeze the hardware.
choices.result: Under load, app processes and Postgres now thrash each other for memory. The site doesn't slow down anymore — it falls over.
choices.lesson: Resources shared between app and database means neither can be tuned, scaled, or trusted.

title: The Traffic Cop
story: A festival sale doubles your traffic overnight. Your single app server saturates; requests queue, time out, retry, and make everything worse.
You need more than one server. You need someone to stand at the door and route the crowd.

scenes.prompt: The queue is backing up. What's the move?

choices.label: Load balancer + a pool of identical app servers
choices.detail: Horizontal scaling: cheap machines, added or removed behind one front door.
choices.result: Three small servers behind an nginx load balancer. Traffic spikes now mean adding a box, not praying. One server dying barely registers.
choices.lesson: Horizontal scaling is the only long-term path to high availability and massive scale.

choices.label: Migrate to one giant monster server
choices.detail: 64 cores of raw denial that horizontal scaling exists.
choices.result: It handles the sale. Then a kernel panic during the next one takes down 100% of your capacity, because all of your eggs were always in one basket.
choices.lesson: One big server is a single point of failure wearing a crown.

choices.label: Throttle new signups until things calm down
choices.detail: Protect the server. Alienate the market.
choices.result: The site survives, but screenshots of 'Signups Paused' spread through seller groups. Your competitors' sales teams screenshot them too.
choices.lesson: Turning away demand protects infrastructure but taxes growth — treat it as a last resort, not a strategy.

title: The Bouncer at the Database Club
tagline: Read replicas — and the lag they hide
story: Reads outnumber writes twenty to one, and they all hit the primary. CPU flatlines at 100% every evening.
Replicas can absorb reads... but replication takes time. Somewhere between the write and the read, Priya updates her necklace price and refreshes her store.

scenes.prompt: Replicas are going in. How do you handle the lag?

choices.label: Replicas + read-your-writes session pinning
choices.detail: After a write, route that user's reads to the primary briefly. Slower to build, correct from day one.
choices.result: Reads drop off the primary, and nobody ever sees stale data. This is Priya's VIP pass: her writes always read back true.
choices.lesson: Read replicas are a huge performance win — but replication lag is real. Read-your-writes consistency must be designed, not hoped for.

choices.label: Replicas everywhere, don't overthink it
choices.detail: Round-robin all queries. Maximum speed, minimum ceremony.
choices.result: The primary finally breathes. Somewhere out there, a timer starts ticking on a support ticket titled 'my prices changed back?!'
choices.lesson: A replica that serves yesterday's data isn't a database, it's a rumor. Lag is not an edge case — it's Tuesday.

choices.label: Cache hot rows in app memory instead
choices.detail: No new servers. Just a dictionary that quietly becomes load-bearing.
choices.result: Fast — on the one server holding the cache. The other two serve different data. In-memory state on a pool of servers is a bug factory.
choices.lesson: State scattered across horizontally scaled machines must be centralized or made consistent — not improvised.

title: "Don't Test on Prod, Bro!"
story: A Friday deploy — tested only by shipping it — takes checkout down for two hours. The fix was one line. So was the mistake.
The team is scared of deploys now. Scared teams deploy less, and deployments that happen rarely hurt more.

scenes.prompt: How does deployment work from now on?

choices.label: Build staging and make it mandatory
choices.detail: A production twin where releases rehearse before they perform. Nothing reaches prod unseen.
choices.result: Deploys become boring, which is the highest compliment a deploy can receive. The team ships twice as often, at half the heart rate.
choices.lesson: A staging environment is a non-negotiable insurance policy against self-inflicted outages.

choices.label: Deploy manually at 2 AM when traffic is low
choices.detail: Careful hands, quiet hours, held breath.
choices.result: It mostly works. The team starts flinching at release time, and 'deploy' and 'incident' start appearing in the same sentences.
choices.lesson: Low-traffic deploys reduce blast radius but not risk. Fear-driven process scales worse than infrastructure.

choices.label: Freeze all releases until further notice
choices.detail: If nothing ships, nothing breaks. Also nothing improves.
choices.result: Six weeks of frozen progress while competitors ship daily. The freeze ends when the CEO finds out and unfreezes it personally.
choices.lesson: You cannot freeze your way to stability — only automate your way there.

title: The Need for Speed
story: Analytics shows the same fifty product queries running thousands of times per minute. Postgres is a genius being asked to recite the phone book all day.
Pages take 800ms. Every 100ms of latency measurably bleeds conversions.

choices.label: Redis for hot reads — with an invalidation plan
choices.detail: Catalog pages served from memory in ~2ms. Writes bust keys deliberately, not accidentally.
choices.result: p95 drops under 120ms. The site feels instant, conversion ticks up, and Postgres stops being the bottleneck of every request.
choices.lesson: Speed is a feature. A slow website is a broken website — and caching is the most powerful tool for speed.

choices.label: Throw more replicas at it
choices.detail: If reads are slow, add readers. Hardware is a strategy.
choices.result: Better, but every request still crosses the network to SQL for data that hasn't changed in hours. You're paying rent on brute force.
choices.lesson: Caching answers once so the database never has to. Replicas answer the same slow way, in parallel.

choices.label: Compress images and call it optimized
choices.detail: Cheap wins only.
choices.result: Product photos snap in faster. The dynamic pages are still glacial. Half a fix is still half broken.
choices.lesson: Optimizing what's visible while ignoring what's measured is decoration, not engineering.

title: Breaking the Monolith
story: Twelve engineers, one codebase, one deploy train everyone waits for. A typo in search blocks a checkout fix for hours.
Someone suggests rewriting the whole thing from scratch as microservices. It's the most dangerous sentence in software.

scenes.prompt: How do you carve up the monolith?

choices.label: Strangler fig: extract catalog service gradually
choices.detail: Route catalog traffic to a new service, piece by piece, while the old code keeps working underneath.
choices.result: Months later the catalog lives independently, deploys in minutes, and the monolith quietly shrinks. Nobody remembers the big bang everyone feared.
choices.lesson: Never rewrite a complex system from scratch — migrate piece by piece, strangler-fig style.

choices.label: Full rewrite into microservices, six-month freeze
choices.detail: Clean slate. Green fields. Famous last words.
choices.result: Feature work stops. The rewrite discovers requirements nobody documented. Nine months in, you run two systems badly instead of one well.
choices.lesson: Rewrites trade known debt for unknown risk — and the interest rate is brutal.

choices.label: Stay monolithic. Optimize hard instead.
choices.detail: Modularize inside, keep one deploy. Refuse the fashion.
choices.result: Deploys stay coupled and risky, but disciplined module boundaries help. For now, the pain stays manageable. Barely.
choices.lesson: Microservices solve organizational scaling problems — if you don't have that problem yet, don't borrow it.

title: The Unbreakable Promise
story: With two services, 'order placed' travels over HTTP. During a network blip, forty orders vanish between services. Finance reconciles against the payment gateway and finds holes.
An order is a promise to a customer. Promises need a system that cannot forget.

scenes.prompt: How do services exchange events from here on?

choices.label: Kafka event bus + idempotent consumers
choices.detail: Orders written to a durable log, consumed reliably, safe to redeliver. Losing an order becomes structurally impossible.
choices.result: Every order event lands in a replicated log. Consumers crash, catch up, and never lose count. Finance closes the month without a single mystery hole.
choices.lesson: A simple messaging hop is a single point of failure. Durable logs with idempotent consumers make lost orders impossible, not unlikely.

choices.label: Write to both services synchronously, always
choices.detail: Two databases, updated in sequence, fingers crossed.
choices.result: When the second write fails after the first succeeds, you've built distributed inconsistency with extra steps — now with pagers attached.
choices.lesson: Dual writes aren't atomicity, they're two chances to fail. Consistency across services needs a protocol, not optimism.

choices.label: Cron job that retries failed orders every few minutes
choices.detail: A band-aid with a scheduler.
choices.result: Most gaps close themselves. The ones that don't become 2 AM archaeology digs through logs, matching timestamps by hand.
choices.lesson: Reliability patched outside the system decays; reliability designed into the system compounds.
